etymology: From the Greek Andronikos, “man of victory” or “conqueror of men.”
biblical_def: Andronicus is one of the saints Paul greets in the closing chapter of Romans, and the apostle heaps four honors on him in a single breath. He calls him kinsman — a fellow Israelite, perhaps a near relation — and fellowprisoner, one who had shared a cell for the gospel’s sake. He says he was “of note among the apostles,” well known and esteemed in the company of the gospel’s first heralds, and, most movingly, that he was “in Christ before me,” converted before the Damascus road brought Saul to his knees. Here is a man older in the faith than Paul himself, who had borne chains and earned a name in the early church, yet whom Scripture mentions only once. He is not a pillar named in every epistle; he is an honored, hidden servant whom the Spirit thought worth remembering forever. The Reformed reader marks the dignity of being greeted by name in the Word of God. Andronicus did not seek a monument; he simply suffered and laboured in Christ, and the Holy Ghost engraved his name into the eternal record. His one verse rebukes our hunger for visible greatness. To be early in Christ, faithful in prison, and beloved by an apostle is glory enough, though the world never learn the name.
webster_summary: A Jewish believer and kinsman of Paul, his fellow-prisoner, of note among the apostles, and in Christ before Paul himself.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering from Andronicus is the worth of the hidden, faithful saint — the believer who bears chains for the gospel and earns no headline, yet whose name God Himself sets down in Scripture. Andronicus was in Christ before Paul, a fellowprisoner, of note among the apostles, and we know nothing else of him. That single verse is his eternal monument.

Such a life rebukes the modern itch for visibility and platform. The early church was built not chiefly by the famous but by men like Andronicus, who counted bonds for Christ a privilege and asked for no record but heaven’s. To be early in the faith, faithful in prison, and beloved by an apostle is a fuller honor than the world’s applause could ever give.

etymology: From the Latin Ampliatus, “enlarged” or “extended,” a common slave-name in the Roman world.
biblical_def: Amplias — the fuller Latin form is Ampliatus — is greeted by Paul with the tender phrase “my beloved in the Lord.” The name was an ordinary one among Roman slaves and freedmen, and many believe this Amplias was a man of humble or servile station. Yet to Paul he is no nobody; he is beloved, and beloved precisely “in the Lord,” for the love that binds the church is not the affection of natural kinship or social rank but the bond of Christ that joins the meanest slave to the chief of apostles as a brother. The world reckoned such a man property; the gospel reckoned him a beloved son of God. Here is the leveling power of grace: in Christ there is neither bond nor free, and a slave in Caesar’s Rome could be dearer to Paul than any senator. The Reformed reader sees in Amplias the dignity that the gospel confers on the lowly. He held no office that we know, performed no deed Scripture records save being loved; and that is enough. The Spirit thought it worth eternal mention that one obscure believer, perhaps a bondman, was beloved in the Lord. His name reminds the church that Christ’s family is gathered from the back streets and slave-quarters as truly as from the great houses, and that to be beloved in the Lord is the highest of all titles.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from Amplias is the leveling, dignifying power of the gospel. A man bearing a common slave’s name is called by an apostle “my beloved in the Lord.” The bond is not blood, rank, or sentiment but union with Christ, which joins the lowest believer to the highest as equal heirs of grace.

Rome reckoned such men chattel; heaven reckoned them sons. The single verse that names Amplias rebukes every estimate of worth drawn from station or usefulness to the world. To be beloved in the Lord is the noblest of titles, and it is freely given to the obscure. The church is gathered from slave-quarter and senate alike, and Christ owns each as His own.

etymology: From the Latin urbanus, “of the city, refined, courteous,” from urbs, a city.
biblical_def: Urbanus — rendered “Urbane” in the Authorized Version — is greeted by Paul as “our helper in Christ.” The change of pronoun is striking: where Paul calls Amplias “my beloved,” he calls Urbane “our helper,” a fellow-worker shared by the whole apostolic company. The Greek word behind “helper” is the same root from which we get the title of a fellow laborer, one who toils alongside in the gospel. Urbane was no spectator in the early church but a working hand, a man who put his shoulder to the common task of spreading and serving the Word. The name, like Amplias, was common among Roman slaves and freedmen, and so again we meet a humble saint exalted by his usefulness in Christ. The Reformed reader notes that Urbane is honored not for office or eloquence but for help — the unglamorous, indispensable labor that keeps gospel work moving forward. The kingdom advances on the backs of such helpers, men who carry, mend, host, fund, and serve without seeking the front. Urbane appears only here, his single verse a testimony that faithful helping is never forgotten by the Lord whose work it serves. His name calls the church to value the laborer over the celebrity, and to count it honor enough to be reckoned a helper in Christ.

etymology: From the Greek stachys, “an ear of grain” or “head of corn.”
biblical_def: Stachys is greeted by Paul in the same breath as Urbane, with the simple, warm address, “and Stachys my beloved.” His name means “an ear of corn,” a humble and fruitful image, and like the other names in this list it was uncommon and often borne by slaves or freedmen in the imperial household. Of Stachys we know nothing beyond this one word of love. He held no recorded office, spoke no recorded sermon, performed no recorded deed; he is simply beloved of the apostle. Yet that single designation is a treasure, for to be beloved by Paul was to be beloved in the Lord, and to be named in the inspired Word is to be remembered as long as the Word endures. The Reformed reader sees in Stachys the abundant grace of God that gathers obscure believers from the corners of pagan Rome and binds them in affection to the great apostle. His name, an ear of ripened grain, fittingly pictures a soul brought to fruitfulness by the gospel. Stachys did nothing the world would record, yet the Spirit recorded his name and Paul’s love for him, and that is glory. He stands as a witness that the worth of a saint is not measured by deeds the world can see, but by union with Christ and the love of the brethren, which God Himself thought worth setting down forever.

etymology: A Greek name, Apelles, of uncertain meaning, borne by a noted painter of antiquity and here by a Roman believer.
biblical_def: Apelles is greeted by Paul with a phrase that sets him apart: “Apelles approved in Christ.” The word “approved” renders a Greek term meaning tested and found genuine, as metal is proved in the fire and shown to be true coin. Apelles, then, was a tried believer, one whose faith had passed through trial and emerged proven. We are told nothing of the trial itself — whether persecution, temptation, hardship, or the long testing of years — but we are told its result: he stood approved, and approved “in Christ,” for it is only in union with the Savior that any trial yields such fruit. The Reformed reader hears in this commendation the doctrine of perseverance, for the saints whom God justifies He also keeps, and their tested faith is the evidence of His preserving grace. Apelles is otherwise unknown; his single verse is his entire biography. Yet what a verse to bear — not “approved by men” or “approved by the church” but “approved in Christ,” the only approval that finally counts. His name calls believers to seek not the world’s estimate but Christ’s, and to remember that the faith worth having is the faith that has been proved. To be approved in Christ, though the world never test or know us, is to share the verdict of God Himself, which no trial can overturn and no time erase.

Apelles stood proved in trial, like coin tried in the fire, and Paul commends him by this single, weighty word.

Here is the doctrine of perseverance in miniature: the saints whom God justifies He keeps, and their proven faith is the evidence of His preserving grace. The world chases the approval of men; Scripture honors the man approved in Christ. To bear that verdict, though no one on earth ever test or know us, is to share the judgment of God, which stands forever.

etymology: From the Greek Tryphaina, “delicate” or “dainty,” from tryphe, luxury or softness.
biblical_def: Tryphena is one of two women, paired with Tryphosa, whom Paul greets as those “who labour in the Lord.” The two names spring from the same root and were likely sisters, perhaps even twins, and both bear a name meaning “delicate” or “dainty” — names that speak of ease and luxury. Yet Paul commends them not for delicacy but for labor, the Greek word denoting toil to the point of weariness, the sweat of hard and wearing work. Here is a gentle irony the Spirit surely intended: women named for softness are honored for strenuous gospel labor. They did not coast on the comfort their names suggested; they worked, and worked in the Lord. The Reformed reader marks the dignity Scripture gives to faithful women laboring within their God-appointed sphere — serving the saints, showing hospitality, teaching the younger women, and bearing the daily, wearing work that sustains the body of Christ. Such labor is no lesser thing for being often unseen. Tryphena and Tryphosa appear only in this single verse, their names joined forever in the record of those who toiled for the gospel. They sought no office and grasped no rule that was not theirs, but they laboured in the Lord, and the Spirit set their names down as an honor. Their witness rebukes any notion that the hidden, wearying service of faithful women is small in the eyes of God.

etymology: From the Greek Tryphosa, “delicate” or “living delicately,” from tryphe, luxury or softness.
biblical_def: Tryphosa is greeted by Paul in the same verse and the same breath as Tryphena, the two women joined as those “who labour in the Lord.” Their names share a root and differ only slightly, which has long led the church to think them sisters, very possibly twins, raised in one home and brought together into the one faith. Like Tryphena, Tryphosa bears a name meaning “delicate” or “dainty,” drawn from a word for luxury and ease; and like her sister she is honored not for softness but for strenuous toil, the Greek word marking labor that wearies the body. The Spirit has joined their names forever, so that neither is remembered without the other — a fitting picture of saints who labor side by side. The Reformed reader sees here the worth of faithful women serving together in the Lord, and the sweetness of shared labor in the gospel. Tryphosa held no office Scripture names; she simply toiled, and toiled in the Lord, alongside her sister. That is her whole record, and it is honor enough. Her name reminds the church that much of the kingdom’s work is done not by solitary heroes but by pairs and bands of ordinary saints laboring together, and that God remembers each by name. To be named with one’s fellow-laborers in the eternal Word, honored for nothing but faithful toil, is a dignity the world’s great can never purchase.

etymology: From the Greek Persis, “a Persian woman,” a name marking origin or descent.
biblical_def: Persis is greeted by Paul as “the beloved Persis, which laboured much in the Lord.” Two things lift her commendation above the others in this passage. First, she is called “the beloved” — though notably Paul writes “the beloved,” not “my beloved” as with the men, a fitting modesty in greeting a woman. Second, where Tryphena and Tryphosa “labour” in the present, Persis “laboured much” in the past tense and with the added measure of “much” — a long, abundant, completed record of toil for the gospel. Her name means “a Persian woman,” suggesting she or her forebears came from the East, perhaps once a slave brought to Rome, now a beloved and tireless servant of Christ. The Reformed reader honors in Persis the faithful woman of long service, the saint whose labor is not a season but a lifetime, who “laboured much” without grasping office or seeking notice. The added word “much” is the Spirit’s own commendation of abundant, persevering work. Persis appears only here, yet her single verse crowns a life of toil. Her name teaches the church to prize the long-faithful over the briefly brilliant, and to remember that God measures not the splendor of our work but its faithfulness and abundance. To have laboured much in the Lord, beloved by the saints, is a record that outshines every earthly distinction and stands written in heaven.

etymology: From the Greek Asynkritos, “incomparable” or “not to be compared.”
biblical_def: Asyncritus is the first named in a small cluster of brethren whom Paul greets together: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them.” He is given no description, no title, no word of commendation — only his name, set among a band of fellow believers and the unnamed brethren who gathered with them. His name, ironically, means “incomparable,” yet he is comparable enough to be listed without distinction beside others and lost in the company of “the brethren which are with them.” Here is the most hidden kind of saint: not even a phrase of praise, simply a name in a list and a place in a fellowship. The Reformed reader finds in Asyncritus a profound dignity. To be named at all in the inspired Word is honor beyond price; to be named among the brethren is to be marked as a member of Christ’s body, known and greeted by an apostle. He performed no recorded deed and held no recorded office, yet the Spirit thought his name worth eternal preservation. Asyncritus reminds the church that the kingdom is filled with such men — nameless to the world, faceless to history, yet known to God and gathered with the brethren. The very plainness of his mention is its glory: he needed no commendation beyond being in Christ and counted among His people, which is the highest standing any soul can hold.

etymology: From the Greek Phlegon, “burning” or “blazing,” from phlego, to burn or flame.
biblical_def: Phlegon is named second in the cluster of brethren Paul greets together: “Salute Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brethren which are with them.” Like Asyncritus beside him, he is given no description and no word of commendation — only his name and his place among a band of believers and the unnamed brethren who met with them. His name means “burning” or “blazing,” and the Reformed reader may take it as a fitting picture, whether or not it described the man: a soul kindled by the gospel, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord. Yet Scripture tells us nothing of his fervor or his deeds; it tells us only that he was greeted, that he belonged, that an apostle counted him among the brethren. This is the dignity of the hidden saint. Phlegon held no office Scripture records and did no deed history remembers, but his name is written in the eternal Word, and his fellowship with the people of God is set down forever. The very brevity of his mention preaches a sermon: a man may blaze for Christ in obscurity, known to none but his small band of brethren and to God, and that is no small thing but the highest honor. Phlegon reminds the church that the gospel kindles fires in the back rooms of pagan Rome that the world never sees, and that the Lord knows and names every one of them, for their names are written in heaven where no obscurity can reach.
